title: Wat Chong Kham & Wat Chong Klang, Mae Hong Son 2026 | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: Guide to Wat Chong Kham & Wat Chong Klang, the twin Shan temples beside Nong Chong Kham lake in central Mae Hong Son, Thailand. See the glass Jataka paintings, woven Buddha, and the evening reflection on the water, plus opening hours, dress code and photo spots.
keywords: Wat Chong Kham, Wat Chong Klang, Nong Chong Kham, Mae Hong Son, Shan temple, water reflection
h1:
Wat Chong Kham & Wat Chong Klang
Shan Temples by Nong Chong Kham
intro: If you reach Mae Hong Son and ask a local where to go first, the answer is almost always Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang — twin Shan temples that share a single wall right beside Nong Chong Kham lake in the centre of town. They look good by day, but once the sun drops and the lights come on in the evening, the chedi and tiered roofs cast an upside-down reflection on the water. It is the most photographed scene in the whole town.

blocks.html: Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang sit side by side on the edge of Nong Chong Kham, the lake at the heart of Mae Hong Son. They are an easy walk from the walking street and the evening market. By day, people usually stop to pay respects and look at the Shan architecture. The evening is the real draw, though — the temple lights up the chedi, and its reflection falls across the water as a mirror image. If you like taking photos, this angle will win you over.

blocks.text: Twin temples that aren't quite identical

blocks.html: A lot of people assume it's one temple, because the layered castle-style roofs of the two run on into each other. They are actually two separate temples, both built in the Shan (Tai Yai) style that drew on Burmese influence from the early Rattanakosin period. The easy way to tell them apart: Wat Chong Kham is the older one, with a large Buddha image inside that locals call Luang Pho To, while Wat Chong Klang sits right next to it, known for its white-and-gold chedi and for the objects inside that tell the Shan story in more detail.

items: Wat Chong Kham — the town's first temple, built around 1827, with a large Buddha image and a calm atmosphere that's good for paying respects
Wat Chong Klang — known for its white-and-gold chedi, glass paintings of the Jataka tales, a Buddha image woven from bamboo, and a small wooden-doll museum inside
Shan castle-style roofs — tiered in layers and topped with fretworked zinc, an identity you rarely see in temples elsewhere in Thailand

blocks.html: If you only have time to walk through one temple, Wat Chong Klang has more to see inside. The most talked-about pieces are the set of glass paintings telling the Jataka tales and the life of the Buddha — the work of Shan artisans, brought over from Mandalay around the mid-19th century, with the colours still intact. Another unusual piece is the Buddha image woven from bamboo, a reflection of local craft, plus a small museum corner displaying carved wooden dolls, the Vessantara picture series, and old belongings of the Shan people.

items.name: Glass Jataka paintings
items.blurb: Paintings on glass by Shan artisans from Mandalay, telling the Jataka tales and the Buddha's life, lined up around the viharn of Wat Chong Klang.

items.name: Woven-bamboo Buddha
items.blurb: A Buddha image made from woven bamboo — rarely seen, and a piece of the local craft tradition around here.

items.name: Wooden dolls + antiques
items.blurb: A small museum corner displaying carved wooden dolls, the Vessantara picture series, and old Shan everyday objects.

blocks.html: This is the main reason people come in the evening. The best angle is across from the temple — walk along Nong Chong Kham to the far side of the lake, then turn back toward the temple. Once the sky starts to darken and the temple lights up the chedi, the chedi and the tiered roofs cast an upside-down reflection on the water. The stiller the air and the flatter the water, the sharper the shot. The prettiest window is after sunset, from roughly 6 pm onward (the deep blue sky against the temple's golden light is just right), and the temple lights stay on until before dawn.

blocks.title: Photo tip
blocks.html: Get there about 20–30 minutes before sunset and claim your spot across from the temple, because blue hour is very short — the light is only good for around 15–20 minutes. If you bring a small tripod, you'll get a sharper reflection in the dark than shooting handheld.

blocks.text: Hours, dress code and entry fee

items: Hours — you can generally go inside to pay respects from around 7:30 am to 6 pm, while viewing the lights and the water reflection works from dusk until before dawn, since you can see it from the lakeside outside at any time
Entry fee — free, with a donation box if you wish to give

Dress code — it's a temple, so dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, take your shoes off before entering the viharn, keep your voice down, and don't point your feet toward the Buddha images
Location — beside Nong Chong Kham, in the centre of Mae Hong Son; an easy walk from the walking street and the evening market, no car needed

blocks.html: The nice thing about this pair of temples is that they're right in the centre of town, so you can keep walking to several spots. In the evening, the area in front of the temple and around Nong Chong Kham has the evening market and the Mae Hong Son walking street, with Shan food like khao soi, nam ngiao and ala wa snacks to graze on. And if you want a city view from up high, you can drive up to Phra That Doi Kong Mu on the hill behind town. Both pair well with Wat Chong Kham–Chong Klang on a single evening trip.

items.name: Walking street + evening market
items.blurb: Right in front of the temple and around Nong Chong Kham, with Shan food and souvenirs to graze on in the evening — just carry on from the temple.

items.name: Phra That Doi Kong Mu
items.blurb: A temple on the hilltop behind town, the high viewpoint over Mae Hong Son, lovely both by day and at sunset.

faq.q: What's the difference between Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang?
faq.a: They are two separate temples that sit side by side within one wall beside Nong Chong Kham. Wat Chong Kham is the older one, with a large Buddha image, while Wat Chong Klang is known for its white-and-gold chedi, glass paintings of the Jataka tales, a woven-bamboo Buddha, and a wooden-doll museum. Both are built in the Shan style with tiered castle-style roofs.

faq.q: What time should I go for the chedi reflection on the water?
faq.a: The prettiest window is after sunset, from around 6 pm onward, because the temple lights up the chedi and its reflection falls across the water as a mirror image. The blue-hour sky against the temple's golden light is the best, but it only lasts around 15–20 minutes, so get there a little before sunset.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for Wat Chong Kham–Chong Klang?
faq.a: Entry is free, with just a donation box if you wish to give. It's a temple, so dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, and take your shoes off before entering the viharn.

faq.q: Where is the temple, and is it hard to get to?
faq.a: It's beside Nong Chong Kham in the centre of Mae Hong Son, an easy walk from the walking street and the evening market — no car needed — so you can keep exploring the area right after.

faq.q: What else can I do after visiting this temple?
faq.a: In the evening you can walk the walking street and evening market in front of the temple for Shan food. If you want a high city view, drive up to Phra That Doi Kong Mu on the hill behind town. They pair well on a single evening trip.
